title: Living ashtpadi 6
hookLine: every comfort points back to a Giver

lines: WHERE A TEACHING GOES TO LIVE.
cards: A grandmother is asked how she is, and before any news comes a small phrase: Waheguru di kirpa naal. By Waheguru's grace. The harvest was good, by grace.
The grandson passed his exams, by grace. The knee is better, by grace. It can sound like a habit of speech, and partly it is.

But habits of speech are where a teaching goes to live. Sukhmani's sixth ashtpadi says jih prasaad, by whose grace, line after line. In homes like hers, the refrain kept going long after the reading ended.

teach.b: Kirpaa is another word for grace, kindness, favor. In ashtpadi four you met it in the child's prayer: in Your kirpaa are countless comforts.
Ashtpadi six spreads the same thought across a whole life: food, scent, clothes, house, family, health, honor. Every comfort, a gift. What does living that look like?

teach.h: ONE CUP OF TEA, TRACED BACK.
teach.b: Take one comfort, a hot cup of tea, and trace it back. Someone boiled the water, maybe you. The water came through pipes someone laid, from rain that fell on hills you'll never see.

teach.h: PAST THE PEOPLE, TO THE GIVER.
teach.b: The leaves were picked by hands, maybe in Assam or Kenya or Sri Lanka, by people who got up before dawn. The milk came from an animal someone cared for. The warmth came from fire, or a power line, or the sun.
Go back far enough and every comfort runs out of human causes and arrives at something none of us made.
That's where Sikh teaching places the Giver: not instead of the farmer and the plumber, but behind and through all of them.
So living ashtpadi six means two things at once: real thanks to the people, by name if you can, and beneath that, jih prasaad, by whose grace any of it exists at all.
The grandmother's phrase holds both. The harvest was good because people worked. And by grace.

how: In everyday Punjabi speech Sikhs often credit good news to 'Waheguru di kirpa', Waheguru's grace, while also thanking the people involved; ashtpadi six gives that habit its scripture.

o: a short prayer said before a meal
good luck that comes by chance

s: thanking grace means not thanking people
living ashtpadi six holds both: thanks to the people, and beneath them the Giver.
kirpaa also appears in ashtpadi four's child's prayer
in Your kirpaa are countless comforts.
'by Waheguru's grace' is heard in everyday Punjabi speech
a habit of speech where the teaching goes to live.

games.q: your grandmother's knee has healed after physiotherapy. how might she say it?
o: 'by Waheguru's grace, and the physio was very good.'
games.why: the phrase holds both: people really worked, and by grace any of it exists at all.

practice: Choose something you're touching right now, the chair, your clothes, the light, and ask where it came from, then where that came from, naming the people you pass on the way, even only as the ones who made it and the ones who carried it.
Keep going until you run out of people, and rest there, at the edge of what anyone made. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, or simply sit there grateful.

wordCard.voice: Kirpaa, grace, kindness, favor. Every comfort points back, through many hands, to a Giver: jih prasaad, by whose grace.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kirpaa, grace or kindness; heard in Sukhmani and in everyday Punjabi speech.

carryVoice: Your line: every comfort a gift. Thanks for the people, and past them, for the Giver. That's day four hundred sixty-one.
